speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before launching into the words I wish to say this afternoon I should like to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), for bringing this motion before the House. I think the motion is so well worded that it bears restating. It reads as follows:
That this House regrets the government's failure to give adequate priority to matters which directly affect the health of Canadians, and in particular for its relative downgrading of the health research budget, and its failure to assume proper responsibility in the area of food and drug safety.
The hon. member who introduced this motion discussed it in great detail. I was really worried about the minister as I sat here and noted his concern about the points being made by the hon. member for Athabasca. I saw in him certain signs which worried me; I was apprehensive about the signs of reactive depression I saw in him. Then when he arrived late for the sitting this afternoon I became even more disturbed. But all of us must have some build-up or be paid a compliment once in awhile and I wish to compliment the minister in all sincerity. Three days ago I had the pleasure of listening to him in Montreal when he very admirably represented our country before representatives of 87 other countries of the world. He was a member of a panel discussing the subject entitled "International Understanding-What can one man do". I say quite sincerely that he acquitted himself in very fine fashion.
For the information of the House, I might say that some 20 years ago the minister was a Rotary International Fellow and indeed a fine ambassador for Canada. I think he was talking in this broad field three days ago in Montreal when he discussed international understanding. I believe we have in him a budding new secretary of state for external affairs of this country.
There are three parts to this motion. The last part deals with some specifics in respect of the food and drug safety problem. I wish to allude to four of these which have entered our discussion. They are listed in a small book entitled "Compendium of Pharmaceuticals and Specialties". The first drug referred to is called Afagon "C", known as a type of tonic to build up people. Among the ingredients are amino acids, arsenic, strychnine and ascorbic acid. The precautions to be taken are the following:
Keep out of the reach of children. Contains strychnine. Do not exceed recommended dosage. Indiscriminate use may be dangerous, especially in the case of elderly persons.
The second drug is one of a similar type, called Hemosomaton. In this case, also, precautions are indicated. It contains iron, arsenic and glycerophosphates. The warning is as follows:
Contains strychnine. Do not exceed stated dosage. Indiscriminate use
June 13, 1975

may be dangerous, especially in the case of elderly persons. Oral iron preparations may aggravate existing peptic ulcer, regional enteritis and ulcerative colitis.
One of the implications in respect of the safety of the drugs listed in this compendium which are available is that they are dangerous particularly in the hands of children. I hope the minister and the officials of his department will look into this matter in some detail.
Two other drugs bear mentioning at this time, because I think the people of Canada are being subjected to drug advertisements that not only delude them and encourage them to spend money but that encourage them to buy drugs which are potentially dangerous.
I refer first to a commonly used facial cream known as Noxzema facial cream. Some years ago one of the leading dermatologists in southwestern Ontario told me there is not one single company that makes more business for him than the Noxzema company. He was referring, of course, to the dangers of contact dermatitis which arises from the use of this particular compound.
The second drug is even more popular. It is known as Vicks. Perhaps you remember having had it used on you when you were children. The father of pediatrics in Canada, the man who built the first children's hospital in Toronto, and the second one also, used to teach us students who put Vicks on children's backs, that one might as well put a postage stamp on their backs. Yet we are allowing and encouraging citizens to spend millions of dollars a year on drugs of this type.
This is some of the information that the department should be studying. But there are more important areas than this, and I am referring to some areas that are of broad concern across the country, matters which cannot be handled by a province and cannot be handled by Canadian citizens as individuals. I speak here of three different areas that I want to discuss this afternoon briefly. The first one is in regard to medical manpower; the second one is in regard to the quality and provision of health care; and the third one is in regard to personal responsibility in the provision of health care.
For a number of years we have been hearing that the federal government is spending funds on trying to determine the status of medical manpower across the country. We are still awaiting a meaningful report on this, and we are worried about the rumours that are spreading that this report will be most inadequate. For instance, in deciding the present ratio of family physicians, as opposed to specialists, to the population, apparently the group studying this matter are going about it in a very simplistic manner. They are identifying the number of specialists across the country, which is very easy to do, and subtracting the number from the gross total number of physicians. They arrive at a figure which they say represents the number of general practitioners or family physicians in Canada. This is a meaningless figure and could not be further from the truth.
I took the opportunity in committee not too many weeks ago of bringing this matter to the attention of the Minister. I told him that, for example, in British Columbia there is an error of some 40 per cent in the figure which they
Food and Drug Safety
present. At that time I did not have the figures with me and I was not able to give specifics, but since that time I have acquired them and I find that it is even worse than I intimated to the minister at that time.
If one looks at the federal manpower inventory for 1973 which was published in 1974, and if one considers the province of British Columbia, one finds that they list a total of 1,946 general practitioners, which gives you a ratio of one GP to 1,217 people in the province. From information obtained from British Columbia we learn that at the University of British Columbia the Health Manpower Research Unit under the direction of Dr. Anderson took a much more realistic view in approaching this whole problem.
It is obvious that physicians who are not specialists are not all GPs. Many of them are doing administrative medicine, many are interns, and you cannot count them as part of the medical work force of the country.
If you take a realistic approach and try to establish how many are practising, functioning GPs, you do this as they did in British Columbia, by referring to the provincial medical scheme figures. They chose the figure of $20,000 gross earnings as the figure they would use as being the average earnings of a person practising family medicine. They said that a person earning less than that was obviously not doing much general practice. They got the figure of 1,270, which represents the number of true general practitioners or family physicians in B.C. So the margin of error there is not 40 per cent but closer to 53 per cent.
I think we must ask ourselves whether or not the government is looking ahead. We heard the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) this morning give us a long list of the accomplishments of governments in the past. I assume he included past Conservative governments in his list. We must start to look ahead. We cannot be satisfied with the situation as it has been in the past. We must also look ahead in trying to predict the manpower situation for the provision of health care in the future.
We must decide first of all how we want health care provided in this country, whether totally by specialists, or basically by family physicians augmented by specialists where necessary. The government has failed to give any leadership on that in terms of trying to delineate what the people of Canada want. It appears to me, and to many people who are looking ahead, that what the country needs is health care provided by general practioners and, where necessary, we need specialists. We must try to determine how many of each brand of physicians we will try to train. Apparently the present government is not interested in doing this.
The manpower study being undertaken should look to the future, not backwards. I hope that when figures come out in the future we will see something with a prospective approach to it rather than a purely retrospective approach. As my colleague says, we should not adopt a purely urban oriented approach. That is a good point.
I want to talk now on the second matter, that is, the quality of health care. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) stressed the need for practising preventive medicine, prophylactic medicine. I

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
think there is some truth in this, but we are spending in this country more money per person than most other countries in the world, and more money in relation to our gross national product, and yet the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands thinks we should be spending more money still. What we need to do is to take a look at the money we are spending now and try to decide whether it should not be spent more effectively. In other words, what we need to do is try to get quality out of our health care, and not provide more and more to people and encourage less responsibility on the part of the citizens of this country.
As the hon. member for Athabasca has said, we need to spend more money on research. Relatively speaking, we have been spending scads of dollars on epidemiological research, clinical research, and basic science research. But what we have been neglecting are two other areas of research, namely, educational research and operational research in the areas of health care delivery. I think those latter two areas are the ones on which we should be spending more funds.
I heard a very distressing comment recently on this matter of quality control of health care. It may be a rumour and perhaps the minister will confirm or deny it, that an American named Dr. Lawrence Weed, who is famous for developing a program of problem orientated medical records, is being offered a job by our government which will cost us to the tune of $5 million, to develop a quality care research program here in Canada. I have heard this both confirmed and denied. It alarms me to think that we have to go to the U.S.A. to find adequate medical personnel to assess the quality needs of the people of this country. I know many physicians and researchers in this country who would be more than delighted to have a small share of that $5 million to study the problems of quality care in medical research in Canada.
I think the Ontario Medical Association not many years ago on their own initiative launched a program to assess quality health care. They bogged down completely because of lack of funds. Now we have the rumour that the federal government is offering $5 million to an American to tell us what quality health care is. I think it is a shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext: The third and final matter I wish to speak about is personal responsibility in health care. When the minister was in Montreal earlier this week, unfortunately he arrived one day too late. If he had been there one day earlier he would have had the privilege of listening to Sir Edwin Leather, K.C.M.G., Governor and Commander in Chief of Bermuda, a parliamentarian in Britain for 15 years, who gave one of the most excellent speeches I have ever heard.

speechtext: He was a Hamiltonian.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext:
He was a Hamiltonian, and he made one of the finest speeches I have ever heard. He pointed out the dangers we are getting into as a society, and that we are taking away all the responsibility from the individual. We are giving individuals all across the country this, that,
[Mr. Halliday.)
and the other, and the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi has the gall to say that this is a right of the people. Of course it is a right. That is a motherhood statement, but people have responsibilities, and I have not heard anyone here today suggest that there are responsibilities which the people of this country have to assume if they want to have the right to good quality health care.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext: Granted, health care is an important factor, and the people have a right to it, but at the same time we have to provide car insurance and life insurance for people. It is obvious that we do this, but in so doing we take into account the experience of people who drive cars. In regard to life insurance we take into account an applicant's general health when he applies for life insurance, and I think the time is coming when we will recognize the fact that many of the diseases of today are due to the kind of life we are living. They are not due to lack of research in terms of physical research, but due to the way we are living in this day and age, and perhaps it is time to consider providing health insurance based somewhat on the experience and the pattern of living some people have in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as a physician, pharmacist, and former medical research official of the pharmaceutical industry, I am again pleased for the second time this week to join in debate in the House of Commons on health and research, and particularly drug safety and our government's fine record in that field.
On Monday, June 6, I spoke about the merits of the Medical Research Council, and now I would like to refer to the proud record of an equally fine government agency, the health protection branch, and its head, Dr. A. B. Morrison. The HPB, as it is called, while knowledgeable and fair to all, puts the protection of the public first. As an industry representative who dealt with it closely here in Ottawa and who was on the receiving end of its efforts and decisions, I can vouch for that personally.
In the early 1960's when the first oral contraceptive preparations were first marketed in Canada, their effectiveness was recognized at once; however, the potential untoward effects in some women were not immediately apparent. In the ensuing years, with the increasing use of oral contraceptives, the possible hazards were appreciated. The widespread use of these potent compounds, coupled with the fact that they are used by a large number of healthy young women, caused concern, and in 1970 the then minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) appointed a special committee composed of leading Canadian physicians to advise the health protection branch on all aspects of the safety and efficacy of oral contraceptives marketed in Canada. Working in close cooperation with the professional staff of the health protection branch this committee published their first findings and recommendations in December, 1970.
It was my privilege to be heavily involved in that dramatic period of our history as the chairman of the oral contraceptive committee of PMAC, the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers' Association of Canada, and a specialist
June 13, 1975

myself in that field. There was dialogue but no special lobbying. The special committee was drawn from top Canadians in their field and chaired by Dr. Robert Kirch, the distinguished chief of obstetrics and gynecology at Montreal General Hospital. They worked hard, along with officials of the health protection branch, and came to the best conclusions which could be reached under the emotion-charged circumstances of that time. In fact I believe they fared well compared with their counterparts in other related countries.
It was considered that a reduction of estrogen dose to 50 micrograms per day would reduce the incidence of undesirable side effects without appreciable reduction in efficacy. This proved to be true. The health protection branch facilitated the availability of such oral contraceptives to the Canadian medical profession.
For the information of the consumer a special package insert was designed. This insert details the need for medical advice, following-up at least yearly, and a warning on symptoms requiring an immediate consultation with the prescribing physician.
The health protection branch also instituted the recommendations on extended animal toxicity studies prior to release of an oral contraceptive for clinical trials and continued surveillance of long-term toxicity studies. During 1970-74 the special committee in several sessions arrived at further recommendations. These included, first, methods for evaluation of efficacy and undesirable side effects; second, guidelines for patient selection; third, duration of use of oral contraceptives; fourth, assessment of risks of thromboembolism, carcinogenesis, depression, hypertension, abnormal pregnancy and post-coital contraception; fifth, indications for altering or discontinuing medication; and sixth, guidelines for information to the profession and for information to the public.
The members of the committee on oral contraceptives also acted as consultants to the health protection branch on problems which involved various hormonal drugs, intrauterine devices and ovulation inducing agents, and provided opinion on a number of other questions concerning medical practice and experience in Canada. This group of Canadian physicians proved to be of invaluable assistance to the health protection branch in service to the public and to the professions.
Next, with regard to the chemical hexachlorophene, in late 1971 the health protection branch obtained data from tests on rats and monkeys which had been fed hexachlorophene which showed that this chemical caused brain lesions in these animals. The branch also received the results of tests on humans showing that hexachlorophene could be absorbed through the skin. Hexachlorophene had been used for more that 20 years without any reported ill effects, apart from local irritation. It is a chemical which was widely used for its antibacterial properties in a wide variety of products. These included lotions, creams, soaps, aerosol sprays, toothpastes, mouthwashes and products for personal hygiene. Most products used for surgical scrub contain 3 per cent hexachlorophene. Other products formerly contained small amounts, generally less than 1 per cent.
The RX Bulletin, a publication of the branch, issued a release on hexachlorophene in the December, 1971, issued
Food and Drug Safety
providing to the health professions information available to date and suggested that hexachlorophene not be used for routine total body bathing for infants. However, if is was considered necessary to use hexachlorophene in the prophylaxis of certain skin infections in hospital nurseries, it should be thoroughly rinsed off.
Further investigations were carried out by officers of the health protection branch, and as a result, on March 1, 1972, the former minister of health and welfare, now the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), announced action which would be taken to control the use of hexachlorophene. The former minister stated that effective in May, 1972, products which contained more than 0.75 per cent of hexachlorophene would be available only on prescription. Manufacturers of drugs or cosmetic products containing amounts of hexachlorophene less than 0.75 per cent were requested to give serious consideration to reformulation of their products to remove hexachlorophene.
Part 1 of schedule F to the food and drug regulations was amended May 9, 1972, and published in the Canada Gazette, part 2, May 24, 1972, stating:
-drugs, cosmetics and devices containing hexachlorophene and its salts may be sold only on the prescription of practitioners unless the concentration of hexachlorophene is 0.75% or less weight to weight.
In the summer of 1972 reports were received from France that several babies had died, allegedly from the use of a talc powder which contained about 6 per cent hexachlorophene. This tended to confirm the toxicity of hexachlorophene applied in high concentrations to humans, especially infants.
In 1973 a soap carrying the brand name "Quote" was imported into Canada. Laboratories of the health protection branch analysed this product and determined that it contained about 2 per cent hexachlorophene. Several thousand cases of this soap were placed under seizure in the Winnipeg area, and the Canadian distributor was asked to recall this soap at the retail level immediately. While there was no hazard from the use of a few bars of this soap, nevertheless the branch ordered this product removed from the market to protect the public from a potential hazard to health from continued use.
As a result of the action taken by the health protection branch and with the co-operation of manufacturers, the exposure of the public to hexachlorophene from those products covered by the Food and Drugs Act and regulations was greatly reduced.
Next I should like to deal with the drug, phenacetin. Several years ago the department received information that persons who had taken large quantities of analgesic products over prolonged periods of time were found to be suffering from kidney damage. This matter was fully investigated with the assistance of external advisory groups. As a result of information received from across Canada, especially from renal units, along with information obtained from studies conducted in our own laboratories, it was felt that phenacetin in combination with salicylates was the major offender in this country.
Some two years ago regulations were introduced to prohibit the sale of products containing combinations of phenacetin and salicylates. Therefore products with a

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
potential for production of serious disease were removed from the market without interfering with the sale of safer products for relief of minor aches and pains. Canada dealt with the problem in a unique way. The United States required a warning against prolonged use as part of the labelling. In Australia phenacetin was removed from the national health service listing. The United Kingdom does not have a warning in the labelling of analgesics.
My next point is the control of drug advertising in Canada. In considering the different aspects of the control of drugs, we are assured by the various steps which have been taken by the health protection branch in the area of regulating the advertising of drugs in this country. This is only too apparent when one compares the type of advertising that appears in publications and on broadcasts from the United States with those that have been produced in Canada. We have been well served by the statutory requirements and the manner in which they have been administered over the past years.
Any representation to promote the sale of drugs is controlled under the Food and Drugs Act, and special requirements are in force for the broadcasting of drug advertisements. Regulations under the Food and Drugs Act and Narcotic Control Act prohibit the advertising of narcotic drugs, controlled drugs, schedule F drugs, limited dose drugs, as well as therapeutic vitamins and minerals. No advertising can be carried out for the treatment of a schedule of very serious disorders such as cancer, heart diseases, diabetes, and tuberculosis.
All radio and television commercials for drugs are forwarded to the health protection branch by the Canadian Radio-Television Commission for examination and clearance. Such advertisements cannot be broadcast unless they have been approved by the Department of National Health and Welfare and bear a registration number. A complete pre-clearance system is therefore in effect. The effectiveness of this procedure is supported by the insignificant number of complaints, four in 1974-75, received regarding this type of advertising.
A monitoring system carries out a review of national newspapers and magazines on a continuing basis, and all violative situations are followed up immediately. Point of purchase advertising is understandably much more difficult to control, and monitoring is carried out at retail establishments such as pharmacies to detect unacceptable practices. Investigations by inspectors of the health protection branch are carried out in all cases that require attention.
It has been recognized that advertising can benefit the consumer when it is fairly and honestly done. For this reason there has been a conscious effort to assist health, industry and other associations to develop and implement voluntary advertising codes for the promotion of drugs in an honest and truthful manner. It is also worthy of note to recognize the progress being made by organized medicine, pharmacies and industry in developing a system for the pre-clearance of drug advertising in professional publications. In comparing voluntary advertising codes with the published guidelines of the health protection branch it is immediately apparent that the branch has considered the requirements of the legislation very carefully in spelling out the interpretations in such infinite detail. These guide-

lines are included in the guide for drug advertisers published in 1973 to reflect the current policy in dealing with drug advertising claims.
In considering the potential for deception, and even danger to the purchaser through dishonest and misleading advertising practices, it is reassuring to note the degree of protection provided to consumers regarding the advertising of drug products in Canada.
And finally there is the drug quality assessment program. During the 1960's the quality and high price of drugs were the topics of much discussion. A special committee on drug costs and prices under the chairmanship of Dr. Harry C. Harley, my esteemed Liberal and medical predecessor in Halton riding, was established to investigate the reasons for such high costs and to provide recommendations for remedying the situation. As a result of the recommendation to amend Bill C-102 to permit the issuing of compulsory licences for drug patents, health professionals expressed a concern about the possible proliferation of drug products of questionable quality.
In May, 1971, the then Minister of National Health and Welfare, implemented the Drug Quality Assessment Program. This program is designed to provide unbiased scientific and technical information regarding the quality of drugs. The most commonly prescribed drugs are subjected to such tests as chemical analyses, product evaluations, and in some instances bioavailability studies to indicate the conformance with recognized acceptable standards.
The QUAD program provides detailed information on a regular basis to all provincial departments of health. Much of this information is utilized in the development and maintenance of provincial drug lists. This information has provided assistance to health professionals in provinces where legislation to permit product selection has been enacted.
The results of testing, plus detailed price comparison information which is compiled by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, are published and distributed to physicians and pharmacists across the country. This information enables them to utilize their professional judgment to prescribe and dispense drugs of quality with due consideration of costs. Since the implementation of the Drug Quality Assessment Program and the publication of this information there has been a steady improvement in the quality of drug products available to Canadians, and there has been a reduced rate in the escalation of drug prices.
In the over-all picture Canada has an internationally esteemed reputation with regard to drug safety and health, and credit for this is in no small measure due to the federal government.

speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) not only on the speech he made today but on the service he provided to the House by bringing forward this resolution.

Hear, hear!
June 13, 1975

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext:
Of course the hon. member for Athabasca is not only well known as a parliamentarian but is also prominent in his professional capacity as a physician.
I listened with interest to the speech of the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), who has had a distinguished career as a veterinarian and was an inspector with the health of animals division of the Department of Agriculture prior to his election to this House. His remarks were based on his professional experience.
There is great concern over the recent revelations by the Quebec Crime Commission, on tainted beef and revelations by the Consumers' Association of Canada on the tests they made of four major fast-food retail outlets regarding high bacteria counts in milk shakes.
There was also the concern raised last fall when the CBC program "Marketplace", using tests conducted by the University of Guelph, indicated that there were unacceptable amounts of harmful bacteria in ground beef in Canada. When that matter was raised in the House the immediate reaction of the minister was to discount it as just another television program. However, pressure mounted, and concern was felt right across the country. Because of the high price of beef and meat products in Canada, people were depending more and more on ground beef as a major source of protein.
That concern manifested itself in the House until the minister was obliged, five days after the revelation, to stand in his place and make a statement. He assured the House and the country that steps were being taken by his department to protect Canadians from harmful bacteria in ground beef. His response was a positive one and he was lauded for it. It was positive in that he made the statement in the House, which had the effect of assuring Canadians that they had no cause for concern. It was also positive because he announced that the inspection division of the food and drug branch of his department would hire an additional 30 inspectors. That gives the department a total inspection capability of 91 inspectors to enforce the massive regulations issued under the Food and Drugs Act. Prior to that, there were only 61. I submit that 91 inspectors would hardly be adequate to enforce the regulations in the province of Quebec alone, not to mention the rest of Canada. These 91 inspectors have to check into food retail outlets, check on the charges of high bacteria counts in milkshakes and, of course, carry out their responsibilities with regard to meat being sold that is unfit for human consumption.
The Food and Drugs Act is quite clear. Section 4 reads:
No person shall sell an article of food that
(a)	has in or upon it any poisonous or harmful substance;
(b)	is unfit for human consumption;
(c)	consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting,
rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance;
(d)	is adulterated; or
(e)	was manufactured, prepared, preserved, packaged or stored
under unsanitary conditions.
That is quite clear. The minister is the only one who has the clear, undisputed, constitutional authority to enforce these regulations regardless of any provincial statute or
Food and Drug Safety
any other consideration. To be precise, regulation B.14.010 reads:
No person shall sell as food a dead animal or any part thereof.
B.14.Oil. No person shall sell as food, meat, meat by-products, preparations containing meat or meat derivatives obtained, prepared or manufactured from a dead animal.
That is taken directly from the Food and Drugs Act. It is quite specific. Just to clear up any doubt whatsoever regarding the authority the minister has to inspect any facility in Canada or take samples, Section 22(1) of the Food and Drugs Act reads:
An inspector may at any reasonable time
(a) enter any place where on reasonable grounds he believes any article to which this Act or the regulations apply is manufactured, prepared, preserved, packaged or stored, examine any such article and take samples thereof, and examine anything that he reasonably believes is used or capable of being used for such manufacture, preparation, preservation, packaging or storing;
That is quite clear. There is no doubt about the minister's responsibility or the statutory authority that is his. Where there is doubt is in the fact that the minister failed to carry out these regulations. More particularly, he failed the people of the province of Quebec. According to evidence given in committee on May 27, the minister said, and I quote:
The inquiry by my officials was started some time in 1973, late 1973. He later said:
-the preliminary investigation by my department started in October 1973, and it was turned over to the police in February for further investigation.
The question arises, why did it take from October, 1973 to February, 1974, to notify the police that there was evidence of meat unfit for human consumption being sold in Quebec? Why did it take that long?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext: Because they were tied up in the dredging.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY

This evidence was presented to the minister. The province of Quebec stands out as the only province which does not have adequate legislation to protect its people from carrion or contaminated meat sold for human consumption.
There are in excess of 300 abattoirs or slaughter houses in Quebec which are not subject to federal inspection or, indeed, not subject to any inspection. Given those facts, why did not the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), in accordance with his responsibilities under the Food and Drugs Act, send his inspectors into the province of Quebec to take samples from these uninspected abattoirs and meat processing plants in order to carry out their own investigation? Why did he not do that regardless of any police or criminal investigation, or provincial inquiry that was taking place in the province of Quebec?
Given the police inquiry taking place in Quebec and faced with the revelations from that inquiry, surely it was incumbent upon the minister to send additional inspectors into Quebec to take additional samples and to proceed in his own right under the Food and Drugs Act and, either through the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Lang) or the attorney general of Quebec, lay

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
charges under the Food and Drugs Act. The minister failed to do that.
In spite of evidence that was mounting every day, and concern that was expressed by the media and on the floor of this House, the minister did not respond. More particularly, there is now evidence of consumer resistence and mounting evidence that Canadians are concerned about buying meat, especially in this part of the country. Why did the minister not respond like he did when faced with contaminated hamburger last fall, and stand up in this House and make a statement reassuring the people of Canada that he was carrying out his responsibility?

Therefore Be It Resolved that CAC re-affirms its policy that all meat destined for human consumption be federally inspected, and
Be It Further Resolved that mechanism be set in place by federal and provincial Departments of Agriculture to ensure that all dealers in dead and diseased animals are required to account for the total poundage of carcasses they handle-

This is the recommendation:
Clarification and Stricter Enforcement of Existing Food Standards
and Grading Regulations.
To avoid conflict of interpretation the relationships between the Canada Agriculture Products Standards Act and the Food and Drug Act and regulations in the areas of meat, dairy products and poultry should be clarified.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with a problem that is of great concern to me. It is with great pleasure that I do so, because for a long time my constituency has provided the health department in our far north with missionaries, people who were dedicated and rendered great services to this country.
Canada can rightly be proud of its health care scheme. Most people enjoy primary, secondary and tertiary health services that are easily available to the average Canadian. But what about those who live and work in the remotest areas of this country? How do Indians and Eskimos and, of course, people in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon avail themselves of the health protection so easily available to their more fortunate brothers in the South. I say that today the really unobtrusive department is the health department for Indians and Northern Canada in the Medical Services Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare. The dedicated nurses and health specialists in that department are actually at the forefront in the fight to improve native health. The responsibilities reach far beyond those of their southern colleagues, and yet few Canadians are even aware of their existence.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to acquaint my colleagues and other Canadians with the health department for Indians and Northern Canada. I will discuss some of the daily difficulties faced by those dedicated health specialists who work in extremely difficult conditions and often in isolation hundreds or thousands of miles from the nearest hospital.
The responsibilities for the health of Indians was transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare when it was set up after World War II. Northern health services were officially inaugurated in 1954 when exploration and development in the Arctic brought deep changes in the lifestyle of Indians and Eskimos north of the 60th parallel.

What was once a modest health service augmented by hospitals and health stations run by missionaries has grown into a network of 14 hospitals, 71 nursing stations, and 223 health centres, professionally staffed by more than 900 nurses and over 125 physicians and specialists. Nursing stations provide the primary point of entry into the health care system. Field nurses, many of whom are specially trained in clinical procedures, provide routine and emergency treatment and health counselling, and refer serious cases to higher levels of care. Public health
Food and Drug Safety
and health education programs are also an important part of the field nurses' responsibility.
Health centres and stations are generally situated in locations where treatment services are available. Nurses operating from these facilities hold clinics, conduct immunization programs, supervise the health of mothers and infants, and encourage people to live safely and hygienically.
Medical services hospitals provide secondary and tertiary health care, and in many cases are the points of reception for patients referred by field nurses from nursing stations and health centres. Not all native or territorial patients, however, are referred to medical services hospitals. Depending on the nature of the sickness and the proximity of the closest federal facility, patients may be referred to provincial or territorial hospitals which are closer or better able to provide the specialized care needed by the patient.
It takes little imagination to realize the immense difficulties which are encountered almost daily by the staff of the Indian and northern health services. I have already alluded to the harsh environment and the immense distances encountered. These, of course, create problems in transportation and communication which only technology can overcome. The federal government's Arctic airport program has solved the worst of the transportation problem in the far north, but weather, temperature extremes, and long hours of darkness greatly increase the hazards of northern transportation. ANIK and TELESAT have improved northern communications immeasurably and have reduced the feeling of isolation. But this is cold comfort to the nurse a thousand miles from the nearest hospital, with a seriously sick infant to care for.
Isolation and the environment are not the only causes of the problems. Many of these problems are the result of cultural and social differences or of ignorance or indifference. In the past, we tried to provide appropriate help and treatment facilities for the natives who had been left to their own devices for many years. Today, these needs have been filled. The enemy, sickness, remains the same, but the means to fight it have changed. The fight will be won in the areas of prevention, of health education and chronic diseases, but victory will remain uncertain as long as our native fellow citizens live in houses without running water fit to drink, a proper sewage system and other services that most of us take for granted.
Since hygiene is an integral part of our daily life, Mr. Speaker, we have a tendency to forget that many native people do not have the same advantages as we do. It can take several years to educate people and to convince them to change lifelong habits, but cultural and language barriers make this even more difficult.
The policy of this government is to encourage Indians and Inuits to be actively concerned with their own health. Recently, we established regional committees, including federal and provincial officials and Indians, to review and coordinate health programs for them. Throughout the years, the health services for the Indians and Northern Canada have aimed at encouraging the natives to become

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
health specialists, and even though this program has had some success, a relatively small number of graduates have chosen to become members of the medical services health teams.
As concerns paramedical and ancillary health services, much more satisfactory results have been achieved, and I would like to take a few moments to give an account of the ancillary community health program which has the well-deserved reputation of being a model for the natives who take part in health care distribution.

Indian and northern health services have recruited and trained over 300 community health representatives who are working at the community level as active participants in the local health team. These valuable workers, native in origin, are known and respected by their own people. They bring irreplaceable local knowledge to the problems of health care delivery and can make the cultural and linguistic interpretation of the health message to the people. By bridging the cultural and social gap that persists between the client and the health professional, community health representatives are making a profound impact on the severe cultural and communications problems that have inhibited the success of preventive health programs in the past.
Not all Indian and Eskimo health problems are attributable to environmental conditions. Last year one third of all native deaths resulted from accidental causes; and it is believed that almost two thirds of all accidental deaths are alcohol related. Easier access to alcohol, the lowering of the drinking age, and more tolerant attitudes toward alcohol consumption have combined to make alcohol abuse the greatest single threat to the lives, health, and wellbeing of Canada's native people. To meet and combat this serious problem, the federal government has introduced the native alcohol abuse program.
Because the cultural and linguistic problems encountered in health care delivery apply equally to programs designed to reduce intoxication, the native alcohol abuse initiative has been designed as a self-help program. It is a co-operative program between the Departments of National Health and Welfare, Indian and Northern Affairs, and the native people. Provincial and territorial governments have also been invited to participate and to co-ordinate their programs for Metis and non-status Indian groups.
Projects in the areas of treatment, prevention, rehabilitation, and education are being initiated and developed by the native people, with the advice and assistance of federal and provincial authorities and agencies knowledgeable in the field of alcohol abuse. The program encourages the development of new and original methods and techniques to meet the problem and overcome the social and cultural barriers that are its root cause. We hope over the next three years to explore fully and evaluate alternative ways of reducing this serious threat to native society and, during this period, to develop fresh and innovative solutions to the problem.

I have been referring to some of the health care problems of our native people. I would now like to review some achievements.

Over the last decade, infant mortality decreased by half, but is still two and a half times higher than the overall rate, which is 16.5 deaths per 1,000 live births. In these last years, the death rate has tended to stabilize, and it is a serious concern of the federal government. To meet that situation, we have enlarged our pre- and post-natal health programs, made up lists of the most severe hazards, dispensed more intensive care and exercised closer inspection over expectant mothers and newborns.
A greater number of native babies are now being born in hospitals. There are more midwives and nurses looking after the mother's health, before and after delivery, and the babies' health is more closely supervised during the vulnerable first year of life. We believe that this, coupled with better child care concepts by mothers and improvements in family environment, will lead to highly satisfactory results. The infant death rate is declining from year to year in Canada. Increasing knowledge, better education and co-operation from the Indians and Innuits themselves will hopefully bring similar results as far as our native population is concerned.
Infant mortality and accidental deaths are the main causes of declining life expectancy among Indians and Inuit people. The average age at death reached the Canadian average, but as a whole the situation is still unfavourable.
Throughout the years, major death causes changed. In 1960 respiratory diseases were the major culprit. They have been replaced by accidental deaths.

Tuberculosis has responded dramatically to new drugs and to new techniques for detection and prevention, but the incidence of tuberculosis among the Indian and Eskimo people is still inordinately high. T.B. is essentially a social disease. It breeds on over-crowding, poor diet, apathy and ignorance. Chronic disease control, detection and prophylaxis constitute a major thrust in the Indian and northern health services program. New and reactivated cases of tuberculosis are closely supervised, and chemotherapy regimens are carefully controlled. Dramatic progress has been made in this area, Madam Speaker, but we have not yet reached the point where we can relax our vigilance.
What of the future? Can we expect dramatic improvements in Indian and Eskimo health, or will progress be more gradual? These are difficult questions to answer, and we would be foolish to expect any dramatic change. Education, social assistance, and health care programs are bringing about profound changes in the lives of our native people who have moved in recent years from being a hunting and gathering society to a society not too different from the Canadian mainstream.
The native people are becoming increasingly aware of the erosion that is taking place in their culture and traditional way of life. But no culture, Madam Speaker, remains static. Culture is a dynamic thing that is being constantly modified as new ideas and tools are developed. The impact of Canadian culture on the native people is unavoidable. The native people can only choose to reject those aspects of Canadian culture that are out of keeping with their way of life or, alternatively, accommodate new
June 13, 1975

ideas and the tools of modern living to their unique society and culture.

The federal government is well aware of the difficulties experienced today by the native people of Canada. We are well aware of the social, health, welfare and living habits problems which increasingly concern our fellow-citizens the Indians and the Eskimos. The federal government is encouraging the native peoples to look after their health and well-being, stressing the importance of participating actively in the servicing and building of the facilities required to ensure that well-being. The health services of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are doing more and more in that regard. I feel that those services give all the help and encouragement the Indians and Eskimos need to attain a state of health comparable to that of the majority of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset compliment the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) on introducing this important motion today. I have followed the entire proceedings with great interest today, including the question period this morning, and I think it might be useful if I took a moment or two to review some of the observations that have been made.
As a result of these comments, and as a result of the minister's actions and responses within his past two or three years in this portfolio, I think this is an indication of how little interest he has had in this particular area of health, and how little positive direction we have received from that particular department.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext:
Let me briefly review some of the comments made today. I noted during the question period this morning that the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) raised a very interesting and serious question about carcinogenic problems resulting from various substances at Elliot Lake. Certainly that would be interpreted as essentially an environmental problem.
The hon. member for Athabasca led off for our party today, making a very excellent speech covering principally the area of medical research and the Medical Research Council. Let me say in respect of the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne), who also spoke this afternoon, that he made some rather unkind remarks about the hon. member for Athabasca and his reference to medical research. I think he missed the entire point and importance of medical research itself. That hon. member placed a series of statistics on the record and, quite frankly, I get a little concerned with this area of statistics, figures, and the numbers' game.
I think we must come back to the very fundamental principle that in the final analysis health care in Canada is only as good as health education, and as good as the very fundamental basis of medical research itself. Let me assure you that if you are weak in one area this will eventually be reflected in the quality of medical care, and I think that is what we are talking about. If I may say so, I
Food and Drug Safety
think Canada has that unique opportunity in that this is one area where technology can be advanced to the point that we could indeed gain an international reputation in respect of medical technology and research. Certainly we have seen this in the past.
I noted a few minutes ago that the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) was present. There have been some who have been very concerned about an announcement made a year or two ago with respect to a new format or a new set of guidelines which the council may take on, and I want to emphasize as strongly as I can that this is an area of medical research. Certainly at the time these comments were made there was some indication that federal science policy for Canada, including medical science research, would be established principally and directly along the lines of national priorities. I want to make it very clear in unequivocable terms that medical research cannot follow that line and, indeed, we need inquisitive research in Canada. This can be supported by many precedents of the past.
I was rather interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) who made great reference to physical fitness. Of course we should refer to this as a lifestyle problem. I was also interested in the hon. member's comments regarding the sharing of programs between federal and provincial governments. I think perhaps this is a little outdated. I would hope that particular member would review some of the comments made in the past that outlined what we would consider to be some of the federal responsibilities and, indeed, provincial responsibilities, in the entire area of health delivery. Again the hon. member referred to preventive medicine, and this also would follow along the lifestyle aspect.
The hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi in his references or comments regarding medical research gave a rather interesting number of statistics, many of them involving infant mortality. What he did not talk about, but which is of extreme importance if one analyzes the statistics and wants to get into this numbers' game, is the question of life expectancy.
Let me suggest to hon. members that they should look carefully at what has happened in respect of the life expectancy of the adult population in Canada within the last 30 years. I am sure they will be surprised to find that in fact it has not substantially changed. It is more important to look very carefully at the causes.
The hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) made an excellent speech, if I may say so, outlining some of the problems in respect of tainted meat and the production of chemicals in the food processing industry. This is very clearly an environmental health problem.
I rather enjoyed some of the comments of the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemount (Mr. Lachance) who emphasized many aspects relating to preventive health care. He also spent some time talking about traditional health organizational services and the improvements made to the acceptability of health care and so forth. He is to be commended for these observations.
The hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau) made some interesting observations. He referred to specific

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
problems relating to the aging population, and again he used the term "preventive medicine". I think I should take a moment to comment on the use of this sort of term. I get a little bit concerned about the use of these terms because I think there is some uncertainty about the classification of medicine. We hear of health care, dental care, mental health, clinical diagnosis, and rehabilitation. I am sure all hon. members could go on and give various definitions of these terms as they are applied to specific aspects of health problems as such. I think this is important because it represents some of the fragmentation and diversity of the problems we see in the entire area of health care.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) who talked about the quality of health. In my view he made a very excellent point when he was trying to destroy the myth that in fact good medicine can be equated with good health. As he so aptly demonstrated, this is not necessarily true. He pointed out that indeed individuals as such have a great responsibility in looking after their own health.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) referred primarily to environmental aspects of health. He talked in some detail about the health protection branch and the QUAD program. I will not get into a debate with the minister at this time about the QUAD program, even though we have had some difference of opinion about the terms of its implementation while agreeing on the principle of some of the findings.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), of course, made a very excellent presentation, but again referred to the environmental health type of problem. I was also interested in the comments by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), although I think I should point out in this case that most of his remarks were related to health problems which are the direct responsibility of the federal government. When we listen to the minister from time to time it becomes apparent that when he is in a corner and does not have the answer, the matter is always one of provincial responsibility, or is the subject of provincial-federal negotiations. I thought it rather interesting that the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier would pick on an area which is clearly a federal responsibility.
This whole subject is rather important, because if we look at the diversity of subjects which have come before us today we will see that in many instances the health system is a system of fragmentation, a very complex system, very difficult of interpretation and rationalization. If one follows along from this line of reasoning one will see that we must identify problem areas, we must realize there are certain important goals to set, and we must outline certain long-term objectives in order to define specific types of programs.
About a year ago, I forget the exact date but perhaps it was in April, 1974, the minister introduced a new working document entitled "Prospective Health Status of Canadians". I compliment him for that document, but I must say in all honesty that from that time on nothing happened. It was simply a smokescreen to have the health program shelved in Canada at the present time.

I must also say I am rather interested in the health field concept. I shall enlarge on that for members of the House. Every once in a while we have occasion to compliment someone in the department. I apologize again for not recalling the date, but I remember an excellent article which appeared in the Canadian Medical Journal approximately three years ago. I recall that it was a Mr. Lafram-boise who outlined the health field concept, a concept which does not solve all the health problems but contains a formula which at least places in perspective the great diversity of complex problems.
The major problem is in respect of health care which involves the familiar doctor-patient type of relationship. It also involves the problem of ambulance services, nursing care, and hospital care. It is that aspect of the total medical care service or medical program that really utilizes about 95 per cent of the tax dollar. I have no intention of going into the many sub areas in this regard which could be discussed. Some were referred to briefly. The hon. member to my left spoke about the health care costs.
We could talk about such matters as manpower requirements, computer technology, and the regionalization of health care services. In the whole area of health care this is the traditional part which occupies the greatest amount of our time and thinking. The second aspect has been referred to by various speakers.
The hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) and several others referred to the environmental health component. I think this is extremely important. When one speaks about the environmental health problem one speaks about a problem which can have adverse affects on the health of the individual over which that individual has no control. This is a field in which the government may well have or does have a responsibility to intervene on the part of the individual or individuals concerned. There are several of these areas which are very clear.
We know about the conventional problems of air pollution, garbage, sewage disposal and so on. There is also the problem of noise control, and the hon. member to my left this afternoon mentioned the problem in respect of asbestos control. I am sure many individuals could give us a lengthy list of problems of an environmental nature where in fact there should be some intervention and control on the part of the government.
The third category of course is human biology. This includes the classic example in terms of medical research. There is the matter of the clinical approach to improve the medical state of the patient. In the fourth category is the life style health referred to by the hon. member for Oxford. He indicated that individuals have a responsibility for health and that we must eliminate the myth that exists among many individuals that good medicine can be equated to good health. I think this formula is excellent because it prevents anyone using the entire area of medicine in order to opt out of any particular problem.
I do not wish to become involved in a number of statistics, but I think we should review for a moment some of the leading causes of death because I think this is important in terms of the health care formula to which I have referred. It is very interesting to look at these in terms of
June 13, 1975

lives lost. If we were to accept the fact that each individual in Canada should live to age 70, then if someone should die at age 31 he or she would have lost 31 potential years of life.
I think one would find that leading the list, perhaps not unexpectedly, are motor vehicle accidents. I have no intention of breaking down the statistics, but others involve other accidents, suicide, cancer of the breast, uterus and ovaries, cardiovascular diseases, GI cancer, leukemia and cirrhosis. speechtext: He now says it was in 1919. After all, he was there. It was in that year that the Liberal party held its great national convention in the city of Ottawa and committed itself to health insurance. It was in 1957, 38 years later, that the federal Liberal government brought in hospital insurance in a bill under which no dollars were paid out, until the Conservative government took over in 1957. It was in 1966, 47 years after 1919, that the Liberal government finally brought in the Medical Care Act. I submit that it was the pioneering done in the province of Saskatchewan in hospital and medical care, and the pioneering done in British Columbia in hospitalization, that forced the issue and finally brought things to the point that the Liberal government had no option but to bring in these pieces of legislation.

speechtext: Newfoundland did pioneering in this field as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO GIVE PRIORITY TO HEALTH POLICY
speechtext:
Yes, Newfoundland as well. We welcome these pieces of legislation, but I suggest we should keep our history straight.
What I want to say this afternoon is based mainly on an excellent authority, namely, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). My point-and it is the one point that I want to make in this debate-is that one of the factors that contributes most seriously to ill health in Canada is poverty. Therefore I suggest that the contribution that would mean the most toward good health in this country would be the elimination of poverty and the achieving of a much greater equality of incomes in this country.
I said that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is my authority. I am forever grateful to him for the excellent speeches he is making in various parts of the country. I will remind him again of his speech on income distribution and the question of community ethics which he gave to the Empire Club of Toronto on Thursday, October 31, 1974. In that speech he pointed out that 20 per cent of our families received less than 6 per cent of all family income-that was in 1972. He said:
Compare this with the fact that the top 20 per cent of Canadian families in 1972 received 39 per cent of all family income.
The minister went on in that excellent speech to spell out the various details and to throw down the challenge to Canadians generally to do something about income inequalities. Then, in one of his later speeches-I refer in particular to the one he made to the Montreal and Ottawa Conference of the United Church of Canada on Monday, June 2, 1975-he referred to his Empire Club speech, and to other speeches that he had made, and gave a brief recital of the statistics he had given on these earlier occasions. But he went further in this speech on June 2 and pointed to the correlation that exists between poverty and ill health. On page 3 of the speech in the text he has given us he says:
I have quoted "Poor Kids," the excellent report published recently by the National Council of Welfare, which describes the appalling waste of our most precious national resource, the children who are our country's future, as a result of the poverty in which they are trapped from birth.

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
The Council's report based on data obtained in the most recent census, found 1,600,000 Canadian children-24.5 per cent of all those under the age of 16-living in poverty. It described the world of these poor kids and documented it with studies which showed them facing a greater likelihood of ill health in infancy, in childhood and throughout their adult lives.
That leads me to pick up the document to which he referred at that point known as "Poor Kids", a report by the National Council of Welfare, on children in poverty, in Canada. I draw attention to some of the facts that are spelled out in that report. I will not go into detail, but on pages 11 and 12 there is a summary of a survey of 222 elementary school children at a school in a low income neighbourhood of one of our larger cities, and the percentages are here as to the number of those children who were inadequately nourished, retarded in their height and weight development, retarded in their physical and mental co-ordination, and so on.
This report refers to another survey in another low income area where it was found that more than half of the 3,424 children examined were physically ill. The same document, the report entitled, "Poor Kids", on page 15 makes the following interesting remarks:
Until Canada's medical research community decides to take a far greater interest in this area we will not be able to say. It is a highly revealing commentary on the directions taken by health research in this country that virtually none of it has been concerned with the effects of poverty. That poor kids are disproportionately sick kids seems to be of little concern to Canadian health scientists.
Then I would like to make a passing reference to the report on the relationship between income and nutrition which was put out by the bureau of nutritional sciences of the Health Protection Branch of the Department of National Health and Welfare, on which another report was produced by the National Council of Welfare. The report itself documents with statistics, tables, and charts the correlation that very clearly exists between poverty and ill health, and the summary-if I may abbreviate what I was planning to say-can be found on page 3 of the report entitled "One Child, One Chance". It reads:
This new evidence gives a special sense of urgency to the need for a broad public discussion of the whole subject of the nutritional wellbeing of Canadians. And from this discussion must come action.
That takes me to another of the minister's excellent speeches. This one was given to District 707 Rotary Conference on Poverty in Toronto on Friday, April 18, 1975, in which again the minister gave the statistics of income maldistribution but did what I have been trying to do in these few remarks, related it to the ill health that results on the part of far too large a proportion of the people of this country. Having referred to these statistics-about 6 per cent of the family income being all that is there for the 20 per cent at the bottom of the scale-he asked what these figures mean. Then he said:
They mean children who are undernourished and sick-who are, in fact, more than twice as likely to be ill as their better off counterparts. They mean youth who can never achieve their full potential because nutritional deficencies or the realities of life on the streets robbed them of ambition and energy. They mean young adults struggling to raise undernourished children while they themselves are ill. And they mean the elderly or the disabled living alone in single rooms, excluded from the mainstream of modern society.

I really do not think it is necessary to have this kind of documentation to make one's point, but I am happy to have this support of my contention, especially when it comes from the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is about to take the floor as soon as I sit down. In any case, I do think that it is a point which needs to be included in today's debate.
I welcome the discussion we have had about statistics and dollars, the various areas in which we are doing things that relate to health and the areas in which we should be doing much more, but I make the point, as strongly as I can, that with all the health services we have we really will not achieve good health for all Canadians until we get rid of poverty. That means doing something about income distribution. That, too, comes under the aegis of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to a large extent. He is talking a good deal these days, when he is trying to fend off something else we are pressing him to do, about a guaranteed annual income, a program on which he is working. Under the heading of health and in the context of today's debate I urge him to push still harder in that area.
That means the minister will also have to persuade the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) of the truths he has been preaching before service clubs and other bodies around the country, and that is that we do have to achieve a much greater measure of income redistribution if we are going to get anywhere near equality.
I am almost ready to sit down, Mr. Speaker. There is another sentence or two in the speeches of the minister which should be remembered. He points out that for all we have done by way of transfer payments and social legislation, the percentage of the total national income that the poor receive has hardly risen at all. In fact, there was a decade between the sixties and the seventies when in percentage terms it dropped. So I add this point to the others which have been made so excellently in today's debate. If we are going to do something to achieve good health in this country, we must get rid of poverty. The minister must work a great deal harder on the whole question of a more equal distribution of the wealth of this country.
