speechtext:
I would like to begin by commenting on a number of specific points which have been raised, but first I will deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Athabasca with regard to the representation of doctors in the department. It is indeed a matter of concern that we should always have in the Department of National Health and Welfare an adequate representation of members of the medical profession. Historically there has always been a substantial number of medical doctors in the department, and I want to assure the hon. member that this is still the situation. They are found at various levels in the department, and they certainly play a very substantial role in the development of policies and programs.
I would like also to say to the hon. member that we have very extensive recourse to the expertise and knowledge of the medical profession on a very large number of consultative committees, advisory groups, and task forces. Sometimes it is difficult, for reasons I do not have to go into at great length, to recruit some medical doctors into the public service, but the fact is that I have generally found that they have been very generous with their time, contributions, and co-operation when it comes to serving on several dozens of expert committees which are in operation in my department.
I would also like to stress that we have maintained and are maintaining an extremely close liaison with the Canadian Medical Association, and that we have enjoyed very good co-operation and good relations with this organization as well as other professional health groups during the last few years.
Food and Drug Safety
As the hon. member knows, we also work closely with the World Health Organization and other international health agencies on a very consistent basis.
A second point raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was with regard to megavitamins. We are very much aware of this situation. I would like to stress that the results to which the hon. member referred, especially by a certain researcher, have not been duplicated by carefully controlled chemical trials. Dr. T. Ban, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill University, for example, has conducted studies and collected results of other studies, and it seems that the views of Dr. A. Hoffer, who supports these particular megavitamins, do not seem to have been vindicated. The drug is not supported or propounded by the Canadian Medical Association, nor in the medical schools teaching here and in the United States. Some may argue that the CM A is only one body, but it is striking that medical schools in this country and in the United States do not seem to be supporting or propounding this particular drug. This is a point of which my department is very aware, and which we are following.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) also raised the question of Afagon "C". As the hon. member knows, this is one of a number of drug products which have been on the Canadian market for many years. It has very low sales on a national basis. Since this product contains strychnine at a very low concentration per unit dose and no reports of adverse reactions have been received by the drug adverse reaction reporting program, we are of the opinion that Afagon "C" does not constitute a hazard to health when used as directed. Nevertheless we regard the inclusion of strychnine in a product of this nature to be of no established therapeutic value.
Steps are being taken to eliminate the sale of drug products for human use containing strychnine and its salts as well as its raw, processed or botanical source. It is proposed to utilize the regulation-making power of section 25(1)(a) of the Food and Drugs Act to remove strychnine from drug products. Drugs will be declared to be adulterated if they contain strychnine and, as such, will not be permitted to be sold. Regulations to this effect will be presented to the Governor in Council in a very short while.
With regard to the matter of nitrates and nitrites which was raised by the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges), I should like to point out that Canadian action to prohibit all but a very few uses for nitrates as preservatives places Canada at the forefront of regulatory action on a world-wide basis. The United States has not yet taken such action although it is moving in that direction. Our research on the safety of this preservative has been internationally acclaimed. Our scientists have served as advisers to the United States government and the World Health Organization in this area. I wanted to take a minute or two to dispose of those few points and then go on to the basic policy questions that were discussed today.
First of all, I totally endorse what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said. He quoted me so often and directly in his speech that I would be hard put to have an argument with him on this subject.

June 13, 1975
Food and Drug Safety
I should like to comment on the remarks of hon. members opposite who argue that I was not giving enough attention to the very close relationship between the health aspect and the welfare aspect of this whole question. It is not neglecting health if you are trying to improve the welfare of Canadian citizens in the area of social security. It would be a very restricted and narrow interpretation of the responsibility of the Department of National Health and Welfare if it were to be seen as a kind of mutually exclusive responsibility. Ideally I think the two are closely related and must move in parallel fashion. It is for that reason that not only did we publish "The Working Paper on Social Security in Canada" in April, 1973, but in May, 1974, released another working document entitled "A New Perspective on the Health of Canadians." This document received acclaim abroad as well as in Canada.
Tin hon. member for Athabaska wants to know what we have done with the latter. I am surprised that as official opposition critic he is not more aware of what has been done in this respect. Maybe I should spend more time with him in the future.
The hon. member referred to the budget of the Medical Research Council. Research is indeed a very important factor and in our document on health perspectives constituted one of the basic thrusts of health in this country, that is, the strategy having to do with biology of which medical research is a very important element.
I do not doubt the hon. member's concern about that particular subject, but I would be more taken by his party's concern if they had shown as great an interest in the matter when they were in office. I only need to remind the House that the MRC budget which now stands at over $48 million stood at $2 million when the Conservatives were in power in 1959-60, and $4 million when they ended their reign in 1962-63.
The hon. member also talked about $48 million but if he looked at other research expenditures such as expenditures in my department out of the health research fund, and under the health protection branch, the non-medical use of drugs branch, etc,-you have to add about another $25 million to the figure mentioned by the hon. member. I think there is no figure high enough that we could boast about it and say we had nothing else to do, but when we are discussing these matters I should present the real figures which when compared with other countries in the world are pretty good.
The hon. member spoke of percentage increases of 2.7 and 13. There again he was playing with statistics. If he takes the figure of 2.7 per cent which is the figure from one main estimate to the other, he then has to compare it with the figure of 19 per cent which is similarly the figure from one main estimate to the other but he cannot take 2.7 per cent and match it with 13 per cent which is based on an increase of actual expenditures. It will either have to be 2.7 per cent and 19 per cent, or 6.1 per cent and 13 per cent. I am afraid the hon. member has got his figures crossed and has given an erroneous interpretation of the situation.
I have a full file of correspondence received from researchers following the announcement of the increased budget for 1975-76, and the majority of that was supportive of the move taken by the government. In effect the number of researchers receiving support from MRC in

1975-76 is expected to be greater than ever before. The impact on the research training program has been increased, and the number of new MRC scholars in 1976 will be 25 compared to 20 in 1974-75.
The problem of regional disparity continues to have the close attention of the council. The council development program is designed to alleviate this problem, and it is expected that it will be possible to fund all worth-while applications for development grants during the present year. This should be welcome news for researchers working in areas which are not those centres that have been traditionally recognized.
The hon. member spoke of cases that had been rejected. I should like to remind him that the Medical Research Council has full authority and independence to decide who gets grants and who does not. In its judgments the council relies extensively on the peer review system and the advice of over 25 standing committees of experts drawn from the universities, government, and industry. When a particular project is supported or rejected it is done on the advice of the peers of those who submitted the proposal.
The hon. member referred to the movement of researchers. An article in a weekend magazine that was quite clearly written before the figures showing the increased support for research work were published, or at least before the journalists had knowledge of them, gave the impression that there was a great exodus of researchers to the United States. I would point out to the hon. member figures that have been reported by the deans of the Canadian medical faculties to the Medical Research Council about the movement of Americans to Canadian health science faculties, and of Canadians to those faculties in the United States. The number of Canadians from medical faculties going to the United States is 28. I asked the hon. member how many researchers moved from the United States to Canada at that time. The hon. member was silent. If I were in his shoes, I would be silent too. I got these figures from my advisers.
* (1650)
While the number of Canadians who went to the United States was 28, during the same period 38 Americans moved into the Canadian medical faculty. Is this a reason to worry? Is this a tragic movement that is occurring? I do not believe it is. For the year 1973-74 our medical faculty had a net gain of ten people. I hope the hon. member will not raise any more such bogey arguments on this issue.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) talked about further extending health service coverage. He said he would like the federal government to extend coverage to pharmacare and denticare. I am surprised. The hon. member has a pretty short memory on federal-provincial relations.
There have been substantial protests by a large number of provinces about the way the federal government has moved into some areas of provincial responsibility. There is an agreement between the federal and provincial governments that the federal government will not initiate new programs without first having a consensus with the provinces. That is still the position with this government and, as far as I know, with the provincial governments.
June 13, 1975

The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands referred to the financing formula proposed by the federal government. He said it was based on the cost of living index. That is not the case. The formula was based on the gross national product increase. We said we would put $600 million into a thrust fund to help the provinces improve their health services. We assured them there would be a growth in the federal contribution to help financing, at least equal to the gross national product. It was to be higher than the gross national product for a period of five years and after that it would correspond to it. For their own reasons, the provinces declined this offer.
We have not stayed put and refused to move. We have had further meetings with the provinces. There has been an agreement between the federal government and the provinces that we will work on a step-by-step approach rather than try to have an overall financing formula. That is what we are doing at the present time.
My officials are consulting with the provinces on the possibility of extending some cost sharing to certain facilities and services if it is established there will be an appreciable cost benefit with regard to coverage under hospital or medical care. These consultations are moving along well. I hope it will be possible eventually to reach an agreement with the provinces in this particular regard.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) talked about government responsibilities. Other members also talked about it. By the way, I thank the hon. member for his kind comments. I am sure his offer of a portfolio is not a double-edge offer. I will take it as being well meant.
The thrust and perspective with regard to the whole area of health that the government published in May, 1974, was that we really want to improve the health of Canadians. I agree we must put more money into research and the services which we have. However, if we want to save money in the area of health so that it can be put into research, we must appeal to Canadians to improve their life style and we, as individuals, must work toward improving the environment. The environment includes the economic environment, the welfare of the people. This is the area where we will be able to make the greatest saving.
If we can reduce the consumption of tobacco and alcohol, and convince Canadians to wear seatbelts when driving in their automobiles, hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars would be saved on health care. That money could be spent on research and for providing better services.
It has been calculated that if only 50 per cent of Canadians agreed to wear their seatbelts when driving, this would save 600 lives and prevent 20,000 injuries a year. Imagine the savings. These injuries often involve months of hospitalization. Sometimes people become handicapped for life and are a burden on society. This is one matter over which people do have some control.
The federal government, provincial governments, volunteer associations, professionals in the health field, and citizens in general should concentrate their efforts on getting this message across. If this were done there would be no worries about having enough money to meet the needs of researchers. We in this country must concentrate
Food and Drug Safety
on our lifestyle and improve our environment in order to reduce total health costs.
I only have a few minutes left. I wish to refer briefly to the Health Protection Branch and its activities. This year this branch or division of the Department of National Health and Welfare is celebrating its one hundredth anniversary. I would not like this debate to conclude without paying tribute to those Canadians who, over the past 100 years, have served as public servants in all capacities in that branch, and have made such a contribution toward improving health in Canada.

The Health Protection Branch is an institution of which Canadians can be very proud. It stands very high compared with other such institutions. As a matter of fact, for those who would be tempted to downgrade the work of my department and people working in the health field in Canada, I would only repeat the tribute that was recently paid by the Director General of the World Health Organization with whom I met quite recently. He said that in his opinion Canada stood among the top countries in the world with regard to health services and its innovative approach to providing health services and improving the health of its citizens.
I wish to refer to some points raised by the hon. member for St. John's East. His statements certainly indicate that he would not qualify as an inspector, and that he would not qualify either as a police officer. Having been a practising lawyer, I would also say he would not even qualify as a lawyer if we have to rely on the statements he had made this afternoon.
He asks such questions as: why did it take four months before calling injhe RCMP? In October, 1973, my inspectors were concerned, and this was well before the report of the Prices Review Board to which the hon. member drew attention. Their attention was drawn by rumours, by insinuation, floating around by word of mouth. They initiated an investigation. They went round and tried to find some evidence. This is difficult. It takes time. The hon. member talks about evidence. The hon. member should know the difference between hunches, intuition, assumption, and evidence.
Even after those four months of investigation there was no evidence. But there was enough suspicion to call in the police and say; "Listen, it seems this is something broader than the 'little mistake' sometimes made by a person operating in this field."
The police were called in, and even with all the power of the police it took months and months before they could gather the evidence. The RCMP alone put several thousands of hours into surveillance-and it had to be undercover surveillance because we were facing a well-organized professional criminal group in this respect. This is not the type of operation or job that any meat inspector or any other federal inspector is equipped to deal with. This is a police operation and this is what was required. The police did their work, and the reason no legal action was taken earlier was that it was necessary to gather the evidence.

That is what the police have been doing for all these months.
My department, the department of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang), and the department of the provincial minister of justice have to act within the law. Before taking cases to court we have to produce evidence. Now we have some evidence, and more evidence is coming out in Quebec. On the basis of this evidence, obviously if there are clear cases of the law being broken, prosecutions will be instituted. The law will be made to be respected. But we cannot go around instituting proceedings on the basis of hunches. We have to act within the law and we must get hard data to ensure that those who indulge in criminal activities are brought before the courts in the proper way.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I did not interrupt the minister while he was speaking because his time was limited, although he did not extend that courtesy to me. But the minister did make what I consider to be a racial slur. He laughs. He should be the last one to laugh.
It is a known fact that there is in this country a means of demeaning the people of my province, and it is known as the Newfie joke. I consider it, as used by the minister today, to be insulting, demeaning, contemptible, and a racial slur. I also consider it to be unparliamentary, and I submit to Your Honour that the minister should be obliged to withdraw that remark.
We in this House come from different provinces and from different races, and if this kind of racial slur is to be condoned the level of debate could deteriorate to the point at which it would be nothing but an exchange of personal insults. I submit that the great constitutional lawyer and advocate from the province of Quebec who made that contemptible remark, that racial slur, should be obliged to withdraw it.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
On the same point of order, Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to both of the speeches made. In his characteristic, strong way of speaking, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was putting forward what a great number of the people of Canada believe is the problem with the Department of National Health and Welfare. In putting forward his point of view he did not in any way deal with the personality of the minister in the way the minister saw fit to deal with it in this House. He did, of course, question his competence as a minister, but surely there is no better place than the House of Commons to criticize a minister's competence. That is what ministerial responsibility is all about. Ministers come into the House from time to time and have their competence and the work of their departments questioned.
This chamber is the place for that kind of debate. I have been here as long as the minister, and this is the place to put forward points of view. But I think the statement was regrettable because it did cast a slur on a certain area and the people who inhabit that area. If something similar had been said about my own province I would have felt pretty strongly about it, cast in that light. I think the statement made by the minister is a regrettable one and I hope he will apologize, at least for that part of it.
In the latter part of his speech the minister gave what some might consider, particularly his supporters, a factual

answer to the charge of incompetence and other things. That is quite within the guidelines of debate and of good taste and manners. But I respectfully suggest that the hon. member for St. John's East was quite right to rise in the context of the minister's remarks and reference to him, which was really a reference to the people of Newfoundland.
It may well be that the minister did not intend to do that, but if there is not a question of privilege here-and there is a great deal to say for it being a question of privilege-then it is a matter that the minister should reconsider. I think he owes the hon. member for St. John's East an apology.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my appreciation to members of the House for extending to me the chance to say a few words at this time. I will make them interesting if I cannot make them short. In attempting to put on the record things that have not yet been talked about today I will pass through my notes, picking out only those areas in respect of which there is some need for comment on the record, and some rather important things about health and Canadian people that have not yet been stated.
It is important that we underscore one of the things which has been expressed vigorously today, and that is the need to work toward a preventive approach to health as opposed to that of simply focusing on cures. It is one of the problems of our society, a problem that arises not only in respect of health but in respect of other areas such as education. We are always looking at how to fix things up after the fact, when it is important that we, as a society, work very hard toward giving the kind of treatment to people in a preventive sense which this society has not yet experienced.
I would like at this time to focus on what I think is a bewitched Department of National Health and Welfare. Let me point out that while the minister was here today, on Friday 13, I still believe this department has quite a bit of superstition attached to it. If we analyze the department we will find it is a department that does not pay
June 13, 1975

attention to the human head. I think this reflects the kind of thinking which was traditional 500 years ago.
When we consider that in this country we have a fairly high level of medical services for a certain segment of the people in our society it behooves us to ask the question: How in a country such as Canada, with its level of economic development, is there still a need for medical services in respect of the eyes, the teeth, and psychiatric problems? I believe this is the result of a cultural and sociological background in which we still believe in the myth of mental illness. As a society we have failed to pay full attention to the human head, and we dispute from time to time that aspect of the human body as a part in respect of which we must also provide health services.
Canadian society today seems to be of the opinion that nature has given everyone good health, and if you are blind or deaf, or suffer from a neurosis, the attitude is probably-so what? I think it behooves us as a culture to recognize that health care means care of all parts of the body, and it is important that we get away from the superstitious practice of long ago in respect of mental illness and mental health.
Another thing I should like to put on record today is that Canada does not have a food industry. We might think we have, but those who think so simply do not know what food is. What we have instead is a cosmetic taste industry wrapped up with colourful packaging, merchandising and advertising. The Canadian public at large does not know what food is. I think it is rather interesting that the field of agriculture has so tremendously outstripped human beings in that regard.
It should be pointed out that it was quite some time ago when the Canadian government passed the Feeds Act, which describes precisely some of the requirements for domestic livestock feeds, sets out guaranteed nutritive analyses, and prohibits supplementary feeds being put on the market without having first been written in chart form and guaranteed as to analysis.
The book I have in my hand is what might be referred to as the farmer's bible. I could open it at almost any page and find it filled with charts in respect of feed stuffs and nutritive requirements of domestic livestock feeds. In the twentieth edition of "Morrison's Feeds and Feeding" at page 988 we find such statements as peanut oil contains total dry matter of 93.5 per cent, that it contains 38.6 per cent of digestive protein, and contains total digestive nutrients of 80.9 per cent. There is a long list of other products in respect of which similar information is given. There is a chart, covering several pages, which contains similar information.
If we turn to another section in this book we find all the domestic farm animals listed together, with the various weights and other factors involved in an effort to achieve a total description of the nutrition required for fattening, lactation, pregnancy and so on. And yet there is no way in our society that a human being can walk into a supermarket and begin to know what he is buying in terms of nutritive value. If one should buy wieners they might be made of beef. One has no idea whether they are all fat, all meat, or what is the protein percentage. What difference does this make? It makes the difference that the people in the poverty sector of our society simply cannot go into a
Food and Drug Safety
store and know how to buy protein or other food items which would meet their nutritive requirements and help them manage their dollar. This is extremely important.
Many people think one can go into the supermarket and buy products which have the best food value, but there is no way in the Canadian supermarket that one can determine what products contain the nutritive value they can afford. However, this information is extended to farmers in respect of domestic livestock.
I would simply ask members of this House how is it that we have considered cows, horses, and swine to be of greater importance than human beings. I think it behooves us to recognize that some years ago the Department of Agriculture carried out this type of a study in respect of animals, and we should have similar information in respect of foods for human consumption so that when we go into the food markets, rather than just buying colour and packages, anyone could understand the food industry and thus be able to purchase the kind of food that would provide a balanced diet.
I should like to turn to another area under discussion at this time. I think that 20 per cent of Canadians can be described as poor according to United Nations standards. I believe this is absolutely deplorable in a nation such as Canada. However, while this is something about which we should not be proud, it is very interesting to note that most of those poor people are Canadian native Indians. I think this is a cloud over Canadians. As a society we simply have not recognized some of the facts. Perhaps I might share some bits of information which I believe indicate how much we think about the health care of Canadians who are poor people. We might look at some things which could be called luxuries.
Some 98 per cent of all Canadians have running water in their homes, while only 31 per cent of the native people have running water in their homes. While 96 per cent of Canadians have indoor toilets in their homes only 24 per cent of the native people have indoor toilets in their homes. Why is it that in Canada on a national average there are only 20 infant mortalities for every 1,000 live births, while among the Indians the figure is double with 40 mortalities for every 1,000 live births and in respect of the Innuits the figure is 70 infant mortalities for every 1,000 live births?
Why do we feel we have a good health policy when we ignore the statistics which show that the native Indian people have a life expectancy on the average of 36 years, and the Innuit people have an average life expectancy of 20 years, while other Canadians have a life expectancy of 62 years? This is a shame we should all bear, because we cannot live in the midst of plenty and ignore a major sector of our society.
In Saskatchewan dysentery is 22 times higher among the Indian people, and typhoid fever is 35 times more common among Indians than among the general population. If we can look for some reasons as to why this is happening-and the department must certainly bear an obligation in this respect-we find that the change in the dietary patterns of the native people may be one of the causes. These people did not always have the problems

they now have. They have them today because there has been a change in their dietary patterns.
Let us take a look at some of the traditional foods that native people used to eat, such as whitefish which is extremely high in protein content. It has a protein content of 25.8 per cent, only 1.3 per cent fat, no carbohydrate content, 356 milligrams of calcium, 106 international units of vitamin A, 135 micrograms of Thiamine, Bl, 222 micrograms of Riboflavin, B2, and in the range of 4 to 15 milligrams of vitamin C. That is only one example, but the native foods that were consumed traditionally contained quite a high nutritious content.
People in the North who, culturally and historically, never used a diet too high in carbohydrates or sugar, are now eating tremendous amounts of potato chips, chocolate bars and drinking coke. I think hon. members would be interested to know that in the Northwest Territories the price of beer all over the territory is the price at which it is imported to Hay River. Yet the price of food includes the transportation costs to wherever it goes, even as high as Frobisher Bay. What does it mean? It means that you can buy beer cheaper than a dozen eggs or a roast of beef. The fact of the matter is that we are giving to people, whose dietary systems have not been adjusted through the period of time, a high carbohydrate diet, and enticing them economically to consume such foods.
I think the House should be extremely concerned about the fact that the teeth of the native people in the Northwest Territories are in a deplorable state, despite the fact that dentists are moving to the area. One person told me he watched a young boy having eight of his teeth pulled out in succession, all abcessed.
Dentists are so busy that all they have time to do is to pull teeth. They have no time to do any preventive work
on filling ones that have partial cavities. The reason is that there are only 15 dentists per 1,500,000 square miles in the Northwest Territories. I think it should register with all of us that we cannot accept this deplorable state in our nation's health, by ignoring 20 per cent of the Canadian population.
I should like to share some information with hon. members. I have here an article which reads as follows:
Food costs in the Northwest Territories ranged from 15 to 70 per cent higher than similar costs in southern supply centres according to a cost of living study released last week by the Territorial Department of social development-
-it costs 383 per cent more a year to maintain a house in Pelly Bay than in Yellowknife.
We simply have to ask, to what extent do we accept that the native people of this country are in fact Canadians?
Are we willing, government or otherwise in this House, to say that there is an adequate health service plan in this country, when in fact 20 per cent of the Indian people are considered poor by international standards? I think it behooves us all to recognize the fact that we will have no health program in this country which is of any level of adequacy until we recognize the full responsibility of caring for all the people, or at least make it possible for all people to have adequate care at their disposal.
